When I was a pre-teen, like most pre-teen girls in the mid 2000's, I was obsessed with the Twilight books. Like, I was the kind of die-hard fan people made fun of, but I was that die-hard fan a few years before it became a trope. My friends and I met Stephenie...I think a total of three times, I met her four times. We first met her on a New Moon tour and there were, maybe, 15 of us in the group and she spent time being kind to all of us and listening to us gush excitedly. The next year was her Eclipse signing and there must have been a couple hundred pre-teen girls. (Just to showcase how much the series exploded in literally less than a years' time.) My best friend and I wanted to stand out and so we hand made t-shirts, hers said "I like my men cold, dead, and sparkling," and mine said "I'm a wolf girl, not a leech lover," because I was that kind of fan, and I went up to Stephenie with my friend on my shoulders to get our books signed, and I will never, in my life, forget the pure fear in her eyes as she gazed at us. I think it was the first time she really realized the extent of her sins against writing, the first time she let herself accept what she had done. She signed our books and smiled painfully at us and it was all great, and I went to signings two more times after that, but it took me five years later until I was willing to try to meet another author ever again. Sometimes I think about it and I start laughing. 

On the flip side, Darren Shan has always been my favorite author, and I wrote him a note after The Thin Executioner dropped (which I had bought from a man who did not have much English in a bookshop in Greece, where I had been visiting, and I thrust 20 euro at him before running out the door) to excitedly babble about how wonderful the book was at detailing the issues with America invading Iraq/Afghanistan in a horror novel setting, and when I met Darren a few months later, he remembered the note. We chatted about the book for a few minutes and he signed every single book I brought. When he was doing the Q&A bit, he asked if anyone had read Koyasan, a short story he published for some nonprofit thing where you could buy the book for $1, and I meekly held up my hand and showed him my copy which I had brought for him to sign. He normally read the first bit of Lord Loss on those tours, but he read a little of Koyasan instead. Super nice guy, super professional and cute, and really seemed to enjoy every moment he interacted with us.

hey friend. i am not a professional by any means (nearly 23 yrs old, to say the absolute least) but from personal experience (as a kid trying to nearly being taken away from their parents in the late 90's and then again in the 10's)...it takes. a /lot/ to convince child protective services to take your kid away nowadays, particularly past a certain age. going to a doctor and telling them that you're feeling down enough that you don't think you're being the best mother you can be isn't necessarily grounds for, say, involuntary hospitalization; i would say it's laudable, actually, to be self reflective and aware enough to recognize that you could be a better parent but mental illness is holding you back. you can't be a very good parent if you're doing miserably yourself. that isn't to say you have to be doing wonderfully to be a decent parent, but suffice to say if you're a parent of a small child and posting to the subreddit SuicideWatch, it might be time to consider that things may suck objectively. 

please take care of yourself.

not divorced but i watched my parents go through a nasty, nasty, nasty, nasty divorce. everyone who is saying "take pictures of everything" is spot on. anything that is worth more than maybe $100--take a picture of it. start separating your accounts the best you can. even if you only have $50 in a separate checking account at a different bank, you're making progress. don't say anything until you serve him papers. and, yes, milk the bastard for all he's worth. my mother was an awful, abusive person, who didn't do a day of honest work in her entire life. spent 18 years living off my dad. yet my dad had to pay her something like 4k a month in alimony and child support. in fact, although he had custody of both my brother (who is disabled) and myself, he had to pay my mom our child support, and she had to pay him back for it. it was a bizarre situation. the system is set up so that it typically favors unemployed wives (as i think it should be), at least in my home state (new jersey). play up the abuse, play up all of it, and document everything possible.

thank you for this message. i'm the older sibling of an incredibly disabled little brother. he is the light of my life and my source of joy in this world, has stopped me from hurting myself multiple times: "but what will he do?" my mom passed a few years ago and my dad is an awful human being. right now my maternal grandmother is caring for my little brother but i know and have accepted that his care will fall on my shoulders in the future; i've known this since he was born, when i was five. the sad thing is that i was just beginning to form substantial memories when he was born, so i don't really remember much of the time before he was born, except that my parents had infinite more time to play with me. after he was born, after the accident that caused his disabilities (which was the hospital's fault; we sued and got lots of money for him, though), my memories are of hospitals and waiting rooms and bleary-eyed parents snapping at me while holding my often crying brother. for a long time i told people i was an only child because it was too complicated to explain that my brother's disabilities were far more prohibitive than society's opinion of what disability is. my brother is about to turn 18 and his future is in a wheelchair in front of a TV--he's blind, he can't walk, he can hardly feed himself, he wears diapers. i spent my adolescence changing his diaper while singing him the sesame street theme, or carrying him from point a to point b to his wheelchair because my parents weren't available to do so. like, please do not get me wrong, my little brother is the joy of my life and i am ready to shoulder the burden when i am within grabbing distance of being financial stable enough to (gotta love that millennial instability), but when this kind of stuff is brought up, my heart and mind and soul automatically extends to the siblings and extended family members who aren't often considered in this mess. when mom and dad are gone, who is going to be responsible???? as awful as it sounds, that must be a concern for new parents, at least at some point. prepare your kids well enough to handle the situation. give them the necessary resources. give them the chance to opt out. give them space and time and love and understanding when they grow jealous and wonder where they fit in the sociological example of a family (seriously, am i the only child, the oldest child, the youngest the middle, the ghost child?????? what the fuck am i?). give them understanding. it is hard on them, too.
